newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FORECAST - Bank of Portugal seen cutting drain rate.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Bank of Portugal seen cutting drain rate.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal (BP) will probably cut its draining rate, the fixed rate at which it is ready to absorb funds, by up to 30 basis points to 6.50 percent for the start of the new commercial bank reserve period on Tuesday, analysts say.
Any move could be announced later on Monday when the Bank sets terms for its first repurchase pact for the period at 1415 GMT, with the result due after 1500 GMT.
Normally, the draining rate and the emergency lending rate, currently 9.0 percent, are set before the market opens on the first day of the new period.
But a senior central bank official told Reuters that when there are changes to the rates, the Bank might opt to announce them the day before along with the repo conditions.
Six out of seven analysts polled by Reuters expected the draining rate to be cut. None of the analysts expected a reduction in the repo rate which stood at 7.0 percent for the expiring period.
Those expecting a 30 basis point cut in the drain rate pointed to the sharper than expected cut in Bank's certificate of deposit rate which was lowered 40 basis points to 6.30 percent on Thursday.

"If the yield on the certificates of deposit, which is a quarterly rate, fell to 6.30 percent, it makes no sense that that draining rate stays 50 basis points higher," said the chief dealer at one national bank.
Another factor creating space for the Bank to cut the draining rate was the expiry on Monday of 311 billion escudos of certificates of deposit which will boost market liquidity.

The only dissenting voice on whether the Bank would cut its draining rate for the new period felt that the central bank would wait because there was still significant short-term demand for funds which was not easily explicable.
The average repo rate rose slightly at Monday's tender, the last of the expiring reserve period, to 7.0125 percent although the minimum was still 7.00 percent.
Analysts said that the longer end of the curve was already discounting a cut in the draining rate.
